notes: CVC words are consonant-vowel-consonant; VC words are vowel-consonant. Focus on what the mouth is doing for each vowel sound. Use a keyword for each vowel. Teach decoding strategies: Touch and Say, reading onset and rime, successive blending. If needed, start with words that begin with consonants that stretch (f, l, m, n, r, s, v, z). Every syllable needs a vowel sound.

pattern: CVC Words: All Short Vowels Together
notes: Time to practise to automaticity. Duration will vary.
Teach both nouns and verbs with suffix -s. Introduce the terms base word and suffix.
Digraphs are two or more letters that represent one sound. These are consonant digraphs because they represent a consonant sound. Sound boxes help to show this.
Digraphs are two or more letters that represent one sound. These are consonant digraphs because they represent a consonant sound. Sound boxes help to show this.

hfw: the, that, this, then, with, than, them, both
notes: Voiced and unvoiced th: both sounds are made the same way, but you use your voice for one and not the other.
Only a few words to use at this point with wh (when, what, whip, which).
Time to practise to automaticity. Duration will vary.
Words that end with the sounds /s/, /ch/, /z/ or /sh/ (s, x, z, sh, ch) use suffix -es instead of -s.

hfw: and, must, help, just, went, stop, best, next, jump, last, want, from
notes: Consonant blends are two or more consonants next to each other that each keep their own sound, unlike digraphs, which represent one sound.
Consonant blends are two or more consonants next to each other that each keep their own sound, unlike digraphs, which represent one sound.
Time to practise to automaticity. Duration will vary.
Suffix -ed can make three sounds: /t/, /d/ and /id/. Added to a base word, it makes the past tense.

pattern: Double Consonants: ll, ff, ss, zz
notes: Rule: when a one-syllable word ends with a short vowel followed by f, l, s or z, double that consonant.
Rule: when a one-syllable word ends with a short vowel followed by the /k/ sound, use ck. Otherwise use k.
Rule: when a word ends with a short vowel followed by the /ch/ sound, use tch. Otherwise use ch.
Suffix -ing means it is happening right now.

pattern: Exceptions: ild, old, ost, ind, olt
hfw: old, cold, find, kind, hold, mind
notes: These syllables are closed, but the vowel does not make the expected short sound: ild, old, ost, ind, olt all have long vowel sounds.

hfw: bring, thing, think, thank, drink, sing, long
notes: ing/ink makes the /ĭ/ sound; ang/ank has the /ă/ sound.
When you hear /ŏl/ at the end of a word, you will usually spell it all. Exception: doll.
Rule: use k if e, i or y follows; otherwise use c.

pattern: Digraph & Triple Blends (str, spr, spl, scr)

notes: Rule: when a one-syllable word has one vowel followed by one consonant, double that consonant before adding a vowel suffix.

hfw: he, me, be, we, go, no, so, she; irregular: do, to
notes: Syllables that end with a vowel. The vowel sound is long.
Rule: English words do not end with the letter i. If you hear the sound /ī/ at the end of a word, usually use y.

pattern: Morphology: Drop the y, make it an i
notes: When a word ends with a consonant then y, drop the y and change it to i before adding suffixes, except -ing.

hfw: make, made, gave, take, came, ate
notes: VCe pattern: vowel-consonant-e. The first vowel says its name and the e is silent. This is one of silent e’s six jobs: it also makes c say /s/ and g say /j/, keeps words from ending in v, keeps a word from looking plural (house), and gives a syllable a written vowel (consonant -le).

hfw: like, five, time, ride, white, live
notes: VCe pattern: vowel-consonant-e. The first vowel says its name and the e is silent. This is one of silent e’s six jobs: it also makes c say /s/ and g say /j/, keeps words from ending in v, keeps a word from looking plural (house), and gives a syllable a written vowel (consonant -le).

hfw: those, more, move, one, done, some, come

VCe pattern: vowel-consonant-e. The first vowel says its name and the e is silent. This is one of silent e’s six jobs: it also makes c say /s/ and g say /j/, keeps words from ending in v, keeps a word from looking plural (house), and gives a syllable a written vowel (consonant -le).
Time to practise to automaticity. Duration will vary.
Silent e makes c say /s/ when e, i or y follows.
Silent e makes g say /j/. When a word ends with /j/ right after a short vowel, use dge; otherwise ge.
English words do not end in v: a word that ends with the sound /v/ gets a silent e after it.
Dropping rule: when adding a vowel suffix to a silent e word, drop the e before adding the suffix.
Two words combined and shortened to make one word, joined with an apostrophe.

hfw: play, day, say, way, wait, says, said, they, their
notes: ai is found at the beginning or middle; ay is at the end. Vowel teams are two or more letters that together represent a vowel sound.

hfw: green, sleep, three, need, keep, feel, feet, week, real, read, please, near, means, year, leave, eat, each
notes: ea and ee can be found at the beginning, middle or end, most commonly in the middle.
-y is added to nouns to make adjectives.

hfw: grow, show, goes, own, know; irregular: though
notes: oa is found at the beginning or middle; ow at the end (except shown, grown, own); oe at the end of a few words.

hfw: high, might, light, right, night; irregular: eye, buy
notes: igh is usually in the middle followed by t, and at the end of a few words (high, thigh, sigh). ie is found at the end of a few words (pie, tie, lie, die).
-ful and -less make adjectives; -ly usually makes adverbs; -ness makes nouns.

pattern: Long e: ie; other sounds of ea

notes: re- means again or back; un- means not or the opposite of.
kn and wr are digraphs with a silent letter; long ago they were blends. Words with kn often relate to sharp points, and wr to bending or twisting.
When a vowel is in front of r, it does not represent one of its usual sounds; it makes a new sound with the r.
When a vowel is in front of r, it does not represent one of its usual sounds; it makes a new sound with the r.
The /er/ sound is usually spelled er, ir or ur.
-er has two meanings: more than, and a person who. -est means most.
The letter w often warps the sound of the following vowel: war spells /wor/ and wor spells /wer/.
There are two long u sounds, /ū/ and /yū/. /ū/ can be spelled oo, ew (usually at the end), ue (usually at the end) and ui (the rarest).
/yū/ is usually spelled ue or ew.

hfw: good, look; irregular: could, would, should
notes: The letters oo can also represent the short /oo/ sound.

hfw: how, now, down, brown, out, our, round, found
notes: ou: beginning or middle of a word. ow: at the end, or in the beginning or middle if followed by a single l or n.
pre- means before; mis- means wrong.
oi is found at the beginning or middle; oy at the end.

hfw: saw, draw, cause, laugh, talk, caught, walk, bought, thought
notes: au: beginning or middle of a word; aw: at the end, or in the beginning or middle if followed by a single l, n or k.
Creates adjectives; means capable of.

pattern: Digraphs & ghost sounds: ph, gn, mb

notes: A word made up of two smaller words.
When you see the pattern VCCV, usually divide the word between the two consonants. The first vowel will be short.
The schwa is the most common vowel sound. Every vowel can represent it. It is a lazy /ŭ/ or /ĭ/ sound.
At the end of multi-syllable words, y says /ē/.
Usually divide after the first consonant, unless you need to keep digraphs and blends together, as in pump-kin.

hfw: even, open, seven, very, any, many, ago, along
notes: Sometimes divide after the first vowel, which makes it long; other times after the consonant, which makes it short.
c spells /s/ and g spells /j/ when e, i or y follows.
A syllable type that is always at the end of the word, the only one where you do not hear a distinct vowel sound. Divide right before the consonant.
-ive means doing or being and makes adjectives. -ion means action or process of and forms abstract nouns; with t it makes the final stable syllable tion, /shun/.
-ure forms nouns; ture is pronounced /cher/ at the end of multi-syllable words. -age is pronounced /ij/ and forms nouns.
